profile.headline: The first human retrovirus discovered, infecting 5-10 million people. Most carry it for life without consequence; a minority develop adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma after decades, or a progressive myelopathy.
profile.syndrome: Lifelong asymptomatic carriage in over 90%. Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL) appears after a latency of forty to sixty years, usually in those infected through breastfeeding, with a lifetime risk of a few per cent; HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) in under 4%, presenting as spastic paraparesis with bladder dysfunction. Also infective dermatitis of childhood, uveitis, and Strongyloides hyperinfection, the last because the virus distorts the Th2 response that normally contains the worm.
profile.transmission: Cell-associated, so transmission needs living lymphocytes: breastfeeding (the route that matters for ATL), sexual contact with greater efficiency male-to-female, and transfusion of cellular blood components or shared injecting equipment. Plasma-derived products do not transmit it.
profile.reservoir: Humans. STLV-1 in African and Asian primates is its evolutionary relative, but nothing maintains human infection except people.
profile.geography: Sharply defined endemic foci rather than a global distribution: south-western Japan, the Caribbean, parts of South America, West and Central Africa, Iran, Romania, and Aboriginal communities of central Australia, where some adult seroprevalences exceed 40%.
profile.incubation: Decades. Myelopathy appears after years; leukaemia typically forty to sixty years after perinatal infection.
profile.diagnosis: Screening immunoassay, then a confirmatory line immunoassay or western blot with HTLV-1/2 discrimination, because HTLV-2 cross-reacts. Proviral load by quantitative PCR stratifies risk, and clonality studies establish ATL.
profile.management: No antiviral alters carriage. ATL is treated by subtype: watchful waiting for smouldering disease, zidovudine with interferon alfa for leukaemic forms, combination chemotherapy and allogeneic transplantation for aggressive lymphoma, and mogamulizumab where licensed. HAM/TSP has no disease-modifying treatment; corticosteroids give limited, temporary benefit.
profile.prevention: Avoiding breastfeeding by carrier mothers where safe alternatives exist, which is what cut transmission in Nagasaki; leucodepletion and donor screening of blood; condoms; not sharing injecting equipment. No vaccine.
evidence: Causation is settled: the provirus is clonally integrated in ATL cells, and IARC classifies HTLV-1 as a Group 1 human carcinogen. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the associated outcomes.

meta.tier_note: HTLV-2. Infection is established and routinely confirmed by PCR, endemic in Amerindian and injecting-drug-using populations; a myelopathy resembling HAM/TSP is reported, but the association is weaker than for HTLV-1 and there is no leukaemia link.
HTLV-3. Human infection detected in central Africa; no disease described.

profile.headline: Retrovirus causing AIDS; roughly 40 million people live with HIV and antiretroviral therapy has transformed it into a manageable chronic infection.
profile.syndrome: Acute seroconversion illness (fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy), then years of clinical latency with progressive CD4+ T-cell depletion, culminating in AIDS with opportunistic infections and malignancies.
profile.transmission: Sexual contact, blood exposure and injecting drug use, vertical transmission and breastfeeding.
profile.reservoir: Humans; origin in SIVcpz from chimpanzees via cross-species transmission in Central Africa.
profile.geography: Worldwide, with the greatest burden in eastern and southern Africa.
profile.incubation: 2–4 weeks to seroconversion illness; years to AIDS without treatment.
profile.diagnosis: Fourth-generation antigen/antibody immunoassay with confirmatory testing; HIV RNA for acute infection and monitoring.
profile.management: Lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy achieves durable viral suppression, normal life expectancy and prevents transmission.
profile.prevention: Treatment as prevention, pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis (including long-acting injectables), condoms, harm reduction, voluntary medical male circumcision, and prevention of vertical transmission.
evidence: Among the most comprehensively established causal relationships in medicine, with decisive randomised trial evidence for treatment and prevention.

geo.text: Worldwide, with the greatest burden in eastern and southern Africa.

profile.headline: A West African lentivirus from sooty mangabeys, less transmissible and slower to progress than HIV-1, and intrinsically resistant to two whole antiretroviral classes.
profile.syndrome: The same spectrum as HIV-1 — CD4 decline, opportunistic infection, AIDS — but with a longer asymptomatic phase and a substantial minority who never progress. Plasma viral loads are lower at any given CD4 count.
profile.transmission: Sexual contact, blood exposure and vertical transmission, each considerably less efficient than for HIV-1; mother-to-child transmission without intervention is a few per cent rather than a quarter.
profile.reservoir: Humans; origin in SIVsmm from sooty mangabeys in West Africa, with at least nine independent cross-species transmissions of which only groups A and B spread.
profile.geography: West Africa, with the highest prevalences in Guinea-Bissau and Senegal, and cases in Portugal, France and India reflecting historic ties.
profile.incubation: Years, and progression to AIDS may not occur at all.
profile.diagnosis: Combination immunoassays detect both viruses; an HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay is required, and this matters practically — HIV-1 viral load assays do not quantify HIV-2, so an HIV-2-specific RNA assay is needed for monitoring.
profile.management: Integrase inhibitors and boosted protease inhibitors with two NRTIs. The non-nucleoside class — efavirenz, nevirapine, rilpivirine, doravirine — has no activity against HIV-2 at all, nor does enfuvirtide, because of natural polymorphisms in reverse transcriptase and gp41. Trial evidence is far thinner than for HIV-1 and much of practice is extrapolated.
profile.prevention: As for HIV-1: pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis, condoms, harm reduction, and prevention of vertical transmission. Tenofovir-based PrEP is active.
evidence: Established since 1986, with virus isolation, sequencing and cohort follow-up in West Africa; the drug-resistance pattern is confirmed in vitro and clinically.
